title: Route-first quick reference card
sixtySecondRule: Before recommending a platform, accepting a trainer answer, or changing a document route because someone on the phone said it will not be accepted, pause for one minute and route the transaction.
firstQuestions: Is it already signed by a public official, or does it still need a notary?
If it still needs a notary, what state will commission the notary who signs it?
What date will the notarial act happen?
What identity method will actually be used?
Is the final output paper, remote/electronic, certified copy, official public record, or just a scan?
Where will the document be used?
Is the destination in the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention path?
What transaction evidence will be retained?
doNotSay: Proof or NotaryCam has the most foreign-signer experience, so that is safest.
The document mentions Georgia, so it needs a Georgia notary.
The recipient said no on the phone, so it is rejected.
Non-Hague means apostille plus embassy legalization.
A scan of a paper-notarized document should work.
The NNA, trainer, or platform said it is okay, so it is okay.
sayInstead: Let us route the transaction first.
The platform is only a tool after the route is proven.
For a new private document, the notary's public-official signature usually controls the apostille state.
For an existing public record, the public official who signed or certified the record controls the route.
A phone comment is not the same thing as a formal rejection.
Hague apostille destinations do not need embassy legalization after a valid apostille.
Outside the 1961 Apostille Convention path is a separate authentication/legalization route, not apostille plus more.
A paper notarization original and a remote/electronic notarial output are different evidence lanes.

apostilleMiniMap.newPrivateDocument: notary state -> notarial act -> state apostille/authentication route -> destination/use
apostilleMiniMap.existingPublicRecord: issuing public official or certified record -> that official's jurisdiction -> competent authority

weak: proactive filter trying to be helpful
platform approval list without transaction facts
stronger: competent authority apostille or authentication result

coachingScamBoundary: Lack of criminal intent does not make bad guidance reliable. If someone sells confidence, repeats wrong authority, launders platform or trainer claims into compliance, or keeps teaching after a source-backed correction, that can be a source-quality problem even if they sincerely believe they are helping.
customerScript: I cannot give legal advice, but I can help route the transaction. The first question is not which platform is popular. The first question is what public-official signature is being created or authenticated, what law controls that act on the transaction date, and what evidence will exist afterward.
